item.title: Ready before it is law: preparing a UK managed service provider for the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: How a UK managed service provider can prepare for regulation under the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill: privileged access, incident reporting and customer notice.
item.content:encoded:
A mid-sized UK managed service provider held administrator access to hundreds of customer environments. The Cyber Security and Resilience Bill would bring providers like it under the NIS regulations for the first time. The goal was to get ahead of it: control privileged access centrally, detect and report incidents quickly, and tell affected customers promptly.

The situation

A UK managed service provider looked after IT for several hundred organisations: small businesses, schools, professional services firms and a few public-sector suppliers. Its technicians held administrator access to customer networks, cloud tenants and line-of-business systems. Over the years, access had accumulated in shared accounts, remote management tools and scripts with stored credentials.

Why now. The Cyber Security and Resilience Bill would bring medium and large managed service providers within the scope of the NIS regulations, because of the privileged access they hold to customer systems12. It also proposes duties to report significant incidents and to identify and notify customers likely to be affected3. In October 2026 the Bill was still before Parliament4, but the direction was clear, and customers were already asking about it in renewals.

What had to be true

  • No standing administrator access to customer environments.
  • Every privileged session attributable to a named technician, approved and recorded.
  • Incidents detected and escalated fast, with a process that can support early notification and a fuller report.
  • Affected customers identifiable within minutes, not days of spreadsheet work.
  • Automation under the same rules as people, including AI-assisted tools.

Architecture

The data flow, end to end

The hard part: one front door for hundreds of environments

Access was spread across per-customer accounts in dozens of tools, each with its own login and its own way of revoking access. The design moved to a single identity provider for all technician and automation access, with customers' systems trusting it for scoped, time-limited sessions. The same principle is spreading in AI tooling: the Model Context Protocol's Enterprise-Managed Authorization lets an organisation provision access to many servers through its identity provider, scoped to users' groups and roles, instead of authenticating to each one separately6.

An MSP's biggest risk is its own access. Make every privileged session temporary, attributable and recorded, and most of the regulatory work follows.

Automation got no exemption. Scripts and AI-assisted tools used scoped service identities through the same broker, with no stored administrator passwords. More on that in securing MCP servers and sandboxing AI agents.

How it ran

Controls were mapped to the NCSC Cyber Assessment Framework, which organises security into outcomes for managing risk, protecting against attack, detecting events and minimising impact5. That gave customers and, later, a regulator a recognised way to read the programme.

Key decisions and trade-offs

DecisionAlternativeWhy
Prepare before the Bill passesWait for the final textThe core controls are good practice either way, and customers were asking now
Just-in-time access onlyStanding admin accounts with strong passwordsNo standing access means less to steal
One identity provider for people and automationPer-tool accountsCentral revocation and a single audit trail
Customer impact map as a systemSpreadsheetsPrompt notification needs answers in minutes
Map to the NCSC CAFA home-grown checklistA recognised framework customers and regulators understand

What I'd do again, and differently

Again: start with the privileged access inventory, because it surfaced most of the risk. Differently: run the first notification drill earlier. It showed that knowing which customers were affected was harder than detecting the incident. Related reading: defender-first AI and patch cycles and an AI copilot for the security operations centre.

item.title: Access by design: building an EU Data Act-ready data platform for a maker of connected equipment
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: How a European equipment maker can meet the EU Data Act's access-by-design rules: product data users can reach and share, consent, trade secrets and cloud portability.
item.content:encoded:
A European manufacturer of connected heating and ventilation equipment collected rich product data, but only its own service teams could use it. The EU Data Act turned that into an obligation: users must be able to access the data their products generate and share it with others. The goal was to build that into the product platform rather than bolt on a support process.

The situation

A manufacturer of connected heat pumps and ventilation units sold across the European Union. Its devices streamed temperatures, energy use, fault codes and runtime data to the cloud, where service teams used it for diagnostics and the product team used it to improve designs. Homeowners, installers and energy advisers saw only a slice of it in an app, and there was no way for a customer to take their data to someone else.

Why now. The EU Data Act gives users rights over the data their connected products and related services generate, including access and sharing with third parties they choose12. Its access-by-design obligation applies to connected products placed on the market after 12 September 2026, and commentators stress that it is an engineering obligation that has to be built into the product3. Separately, the Act's cloud switching rules prohibit switching charges from 12 January 20273. For a product line launching new models, both dates landed in the middle of the roadmap.

What had to be true

  • Users can get their data easily, in a usable format, without raising a support ticket.
  • Users can share it with an installer, energy adviser or app of their choice, and revoke that.
  • Personal data handled under the GDPR, because household energy patterns can identify people4.
  • Trade secrets protected through agreed measures, not used as a blanket excuse.
  • No cloud lock-in in the platform itself, in line with the switching rules.

Architecture

The data flow, end to end

The hard part: ingestion that scales with the fleet

Access by design starts at ingestion: if data is dropped, summarised too early or locked into a proprietary pipeline, users cannot get it later. The team standardised device telemetry on OTLP and placed a tier of OpenTelemetry Collectors in gateway mode behind a load balancer in each region, so data keeps flowing as the fleet grows and individual collectors can be replaced without loss5.

You cannot share data you never kept. Access by design is decided at ingestion, years before a user asks.

The second hard part was the line between raw data and know-how. Raw readings went into the user-accessible store; the predictive maintenance models and efficiency algorithms built from them stayed separate, with sharing partners bound by terms to protect anything sensitive. More on related patterns in OpenTelemetry Collector deployment patterns and data contracts.

How it ran

Key decisions and trade-offs

DecisionAlternativeWhy
Self-service access and sharingData requests through supportThe obligation is about design; support processes do not scale
Separate raw data from derived modelsOne store for everythingShare raw data freely while protecting know-how
Open telemetry protocol and formatsProprietary device protocolEasier access, portability and partner integration
A data catalogue users can readRaw field dumpsData is only useful if people know what it means
Infrastructure as code, open formatsDeep use of one cloud's proprietary servicesKeeps switching realistic as the rules intend

What I'd do again, and differently

Again: treat the catalogue as a product, because it made the data useful to customers and partners, not just compliant. Differently: settle the trade secret approach with legal before building the stores, since it shaped the data model more than any technical choice. Related reading: lakehouse catalogue strategy and the EU AI Act roadmap.

item.title: When the model is a material service provider: AI resilience for an Australian insurer under CPS 230
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: How an Australian insurer can treat AI model providers as material service providers under CPS 230: critical operations, tolerances, fallbacks and tested exit plans.
item.content:encoded:
An Australian general insurer had put AI into claims intake, customer service and fraud review, mostly through one hosted model provider. Nobody had asked what happens when that provider is slow, out of capacity or gone. Under APRA's CPS 230 that is a board-level question, and the goal was a credible answer.

The situation

A general insurer in Australia had moved quickly with AI. Claims intake used a hosted model to read documents and photos, the contact centre used it to draft responses, and the fraud team used it to summarise case files. Almost all of it ran through one external model provider, wired directly into each application.

CPS 230, APRA's prudential standard on operational risk management, has applied to banks, insurers and superannuation entities since 1 July 2025, with existing service provider contracts brought in at renewal or by 1 July 20261. It expects entities to identify critical operations, set tolerance levels for disruption, and manage material service providers2. The board asked a fair question: if the model provider has an outage, runs out of capacity or changes terms, what happens to claims?

Why now. Capacity is not a theoretical risk. Reporting on Microsoft's latest results notes that demand for its cloud still exceeds supply4, and AI capacity is the tightest part of that market. See the tech news update for 29 October.

What had to be true

  • AI dependencies visible in the same register as other material service providers.
  • Tolerance levels for each AI-assisted critical operation: how long, how degraded, before customers are harmed.
  • A tested alternative for every critical use, not a slide.
  • Privacy obligations met on every path, including fallbacks.
  • No rebuild of the applications: changes behind a common interface.

Architecture

The data flow, end to end

The hard part: deciding what to drop when capacity is short

Not every AI use is equally important, and pretending otherwise means everything fails together. The team tagged each request with the criticality of the operation it served, so the gateway could protect claims intake and shed or delay lower-priority work. The same idea appears in the Kubernetes Gateway API inference extension, where scheduling considers whether a request is critical and whether there is capacity before choosing a model server, and can drop non-critical requests when there is not5.

Resilience for AI is mostly a prioritisation decision. Decide in advance which work gets the last available capacity.

Every fallback path also had to meet privacy obligations. The OAIC's guidance on commercially available AI products expects due diligence on each product and ongoing review, not a one-off check3, so the second provider and the private model went through the same assessment as the primary. Routing patterns are covered in LLM model routing and Kubernetes inference gateways.

How it ran

Key decisions and trade-offs

DecisionAlternativeWhy
A single model gatewayProvider SDKs in each applicationFailover and exit become configuration, not rewrites
Second provider from a different vendorSecond region with the same vendorReduces concentration on one company's terms and capacity
Small private model as a floorHosted providers onlyA guaranteed baseline for the most critical step
Criticality tags on every requestTreat all AI traffic the sameProtects claims when capacity is short
Rehearse exit with live trafficA written exit planOnly tested plans count

What I'd do again, and differently

Again: put a gateway in front of every model call before adding a second provider; it made everything else cheap. Differently: build the evaluation set for each critical operation first. The slowest part of adding a provider was proving its answers were good enough, not wiring it in. See evaluation sets that predict production and AI incident postmortems.

item.title: When the customer is an agent: making a Southeast Asian travel marketplace ready for AI assistants
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: How a Southeast Asian travel marketplace can serve AI agents as well as people: machine-readable inventory, safe booking APIs, approvals and separate routing.
item.content:encoded:
A regional travel marketplace saw consumer AI agents arrive in its home market, able to compare, basket and book on a person's behalf. Its site was built for humans and scrapers. The goal was to give agents a fast, safe and honest way in, without breaking the experience for everyone else.

The situation

A travel marketplace serving Singapore and its neighbours sold hotels, flights and activities through a website and app. Its traffic already included price scrapers and comparison bots, handled with blocking and rate limits. Its booking flow assumed a person clicking through screens.

Why now. In late October 2026, Meta made its personal AI agent, Muse, available in Singapore, with partners including Shopee, Grab, Singapore Airlines, Agoda and Trip.com12. Coverage describes the agent building a basket and waiting for the person's approval before ordering, and asking for approval before sensitive steps such as purchases2. For a travel business, that means some customers will arrive through an assistant rather than the app, and the marketplace either offers agents a good way in or watches them book elsewhere. See the tech news update for 29 October.

What had to be true

  • Agents read the truth: inventory, total prices, fees and cancellation rules available as structured data, not scraped from pages.
  • No booking without a person's approval, and no duplicate bookings from retries.
  • Agent traffic isolated, so a busy agent platform cannot slow down human customers.
  • Clear data protection basis for using personal data in recommendations under Singapore's PDPA.
  • One interface for many agents, not a custom integration per assistant.

Architecture

The data flow, end to end

The agent-facing tools followed the Model Context Protocol so different assistants could use the same interface5. Security for those tools followed the practices in securing MCP servers, and the idempotent booking design reused patterns from idempotent payment pipelines.

The hard part: serving agents without hurting people

Agent platforms can generate bursts of searches as they compare options for thousands of users at once. The answer was to route agent traffic to its own backends with its own limits and capacity, so a spike from one assistant never slowed the app. The Kubernetes Gateway API made this declarative: routes can match on headers, such as an authenticated agent identifier, and split or direct traffic to different services4.

Treat agents as a customer channel, not as bots to block. Give them a front door, rules and limits, and they become measurable revenue instead of unmanaged load.

On personal data, the PDPC's advisory guidelines explain how consent and notification obligations, and their exceptions, apply when personal data is used in AI recommendation systems3. Recommendations to agents used only the data needed for the request, and anything personalised was tied to a recorded basis. More on the rules in fractional CTO in Singapore.

How it ran

Key decisions and trade-offs

DecisionAlternativeWhy
Serve agents through an APIBlock or tolerate scrapingAccurate data, control and a measurable channel
Hold and approve before bookingLet agents book directlyA person's consent for every purchase, fewer disputes
Idempotency keys on every booking callRely on agents not retryingAgents retry; duplicates are expensive
Separate routing and capacity for agentsOne shared backendAgent bursts cannot degrade the app
Standard protocol for toolsCustom integration per assistantOne interface, many agents

What I'd do again, and differently

Again: make prices and policies machine-readable first; it improved the human site too. Differently: involve finance and customer service earlier. Approval, refund and dispute flows for agent bookings raised more questions than the APIs did. Related reading: structured data for AI search and MCP registries for enterprises.

item.title: Consent that actually propagates: preparing an Indian digital lender for the DPDP Rules
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: How an Indian digital lender can prepare for the DPDP Rules: purpose-level consent, withdrawal that reaches every partner, real erasure and evidence for audits.
item.content:encoded:
An Indian digital lender collected consent in its app but could not say, for any one customer, which partners held their data, for what purpose, or whether a withdrawal had reached them. With the DPDP Rules phasing in, the goal was a consent and data-rights platform that turns legal obligations into events every system honours.

The situation

A digital lender in India served customers through a mobile app, with credit decisions supported by bureaus, co-lending partners, verification vendors, a collections agency and marketing platforms. Consent was a set of checkboxes at sign-up. Personal data flowed to partners through file drops and APIs built over years by different teams, and nobody could answer a simple question for a single customer: who holds this person's data, for which purpose, and what happens if they withdraw?

Why now. The Digital Personal Data Protection Rules were notified on 13 November 2025, bringing the DPDP Act, 2023 into force in stages over 18 months12. Registration of consent managers applies after the first year, which falls in November 2026, and most core obligations for data fiduciaries apply from around May 20273. For a lender whose business runs on personal and financial data, that is not much time to rebuild how consent works.

What had to be true

  • Consent per purpose, not one blanket checkbox, with the notice version recorded.
  • Withdrawal as easy as giving consent, and actually honoured by every system and partner.
  • Retention that deletes: data removed when its purpose ends, with evidence.
  • Breach detection and reporting fast enough to meet notification duties.
  • Room for consent managers, so customers can manage consent through a registered intermediary.

Architecture

The data flow, end to end

The hard part: proving a withdrawal reached everyone

Recording consent is easy. Proving that a withdrawal stopped processing everywhere is not, because data has already been copied to analytics, partners and vendors. The design treated each withdrawal as an event on the stream, with every consumer and partner integration required to acknowledge it. Tracing producers and consumers with OpenTelemetry links a published event to each receiving service in one trace4, which turns propagation into something you can query and show to an auditor.

A consent you cannot withdraw everywhere is not really consent. Design withdrawal first; recording consent is the easy half.

Partners without event integrations received withdrawals through an authenticated API with mandatory acknowledgement and a retry queue. Unacknowledged withdrawals raised alerts to the partner owner, not just to engineering. Related reading: change data capture and event streams and data contracts.

How it ran

Key decisions and trade-offs

DecisionAlternativeWhy
Append-only consent ledgerConsent flags on the customer recordHistory, notice versions and audit evidence come built in
Withdrawal as an event with acknowledgementNightly batch updatesFast propagation and proof of delivery per system
Purpose tags on data in analyticsOne shared data lake with no purpose contextLets retention and access rules work on analytical copies too
Deletion with proofSoft-delete flagsErasure has to be real and demonstrable
Design for consent managers nowWait for the registry to matureInterfaces are cheaper to add before integrations multiply

What I'd do again, and differently

Again: start with the data and partner inventory, and make withdrawal the first feature built. Differently: bring partners in earlier. The longest delays came from contract changes and vendors without any way to receive a withdrawal, not from the engineering. For broader context on rules across markets, see where I work and how another data protection law shapes AI architecture.

item.title: From emergency patch to modern platform: securing a legacy PHP estate without a big-bang rewrite
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: How a US insurer can find every PHP runtime, patch exploited flaws fast, add tracing and retire legacy apps safely, using a strangler pattern instead of a rewrite.
item.content:encoded:
A US specialty insurer ran its agent portal, quoting tools and dozens of marketing sites on PHP, some of it years out of support. When an actively exploited PHP flaw landed, nobody could say quickly where PHP was running. The goal was to close that exposure in days, then turn a one-off scramble into a platform that stays patched.

The situation

A specialty insurer in the United States had grown its digital estate over fifteen years. The agent portal and quoting tools ran on PHP, alongside dozens of marketing and campaign sites built by agencies, a document-generation service, and vendor appliances that embedded PHP without anyone realising. Some runtimes were current; others were several releases out of support.

Why now. On 26 October 2026, CISA added two PHP remote code execution flaws, known as PHP2Shell, to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog and gave US federal agencies days to remediate13. Researchers reported successful exploitation in the wild2. For a regulated insurer, the first question from the board was simple: are we exposed? The honest answer was "we don't know yet", and that was the real problem to solve.

What had to be true

  • Exposure closed within days: every affected runtime patched to a fixed release or isolated.
  • One trustworthy inventory of PHP runtimes, versions and owners, refreshed automatically.
  • No outage for agents during quoting hours.
  • Visibility before change: know what each legacy app actually does in production before touching it.
  • A durable fix, so the next advisory is routine work, not a crisis.

Architecture

The data flow, end to end

The patched releases (8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35) were available from 21 October2. Anything on PHP 8.1 or older could not simply be patched, because those branches no longer receive security fixes4; CISA's advice for such systems was to take them offline until they could be upgraded1.

The hard part: changing systems nobody fully understood

The quoting tool had no tests and few people who knew it well. Before upgrading or migrating anything, the team added request tracing at the web server. The OpenTelemetry module for Apache HTTP Server records each incoming request as a trace, with spans for the modules involved, so you can see what the server is doing without changing application code5.

A few weeks of traces showed which routes agents actually used, which were dead, and which called downstream systems. That turned an unknown monolith into a ranked list of routes to move.

The first deliverable of any legacy modernisation is a map of what the system really does in production. Traces give you that map for free.

With that map, quoting functions moved behind a routing facade one route at a time, the strangler fig approach6: new services took over a route, traffic shifted gradually, and the old code path was removed once unused. More on the observability side in OpenTelemetry Collector deployment patterns.

How it ran

Key decisions and trade-offs

DecisionAlternativeWhy
Isolate unsupported runtimes immediatelyLeave them up behind the WAFNo security fixes are coming for those branches; a WAF is a stopgap
Golden images for all PHP appsPatch each server by handOne rebuild fixes every app; drift disappears
Trace before changing codeRead the code and guessProduction behaviour beats documentation that no longer exists
Strangler facadeBig-bang rewriteSmall, reversible steps with no quoting outage
Static hosting for marketing sitesKeep a PHP runtime per siteRemoves dozens of attack surfaces entirely

What I'd do again, and differently

Again: inventory first, then golden images, then tracing before touching code. Differently: put patch SLAs and the exceptions register in place before an emergency, not after. The scramble was mostly the cost of not knowing what was running. For the incident-review side, see running useful postmortems, and for the week's context, tech news for 29 October.

item.title: An AI copilot for the security operations centre that analysts trust
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: How a security team can use AI to triage alerts faster without handing it the keys: normalised OCSF data, ATT&CK context, cited summaries and human-approved response.
item.content:encoded:
A security operations team faced more alerts than analysts, from tools that each spoke their own data format. Leadership wanted AI to help. Analysts wanted it not to invent things or take actions on its own. The goal was a copilot that speeds up triage and investigation while every response stays a human decision.

The situation

A financial services group ran a security operations centre that took alerts from endpoint protection, identity providers, cloud platforms, email security and network tools. Each tool had its own data format and console. Analysts spent much of their time gathering context: which user, which host, what else happened nearby, has this been seen before. Experienced analysts carried that knowledge in their heads; newer ones escalated more than they needed to.

Leadership wanted to apply AI. The security team's concerns were specific: an assistant that invents findings, one that attackers can manipulate through the very logs it reads, and anything that acts on production systems without a person deciding.

What had to be true

  • Every statement cited to the events, alerts or runbooks it came from.
  • Read-only by default: the copilot investigates; it does not change systems.
  • Human approval for every response action, with the action and its reason logged.
  • Consistent data across sources, so the same question gives the same kind of answer.
  • Aligned with the incident response process the organisation already followed and was audited against.

Architecture

The data flow, end to end

Normalisation made the rest possible. OCSF is an open, vendor-agnostic schema for security events, with a framework of data types, an attribute dictionary and a taxonomy2, and it moved under Linux Foundation governance in 20243. MITRE ATT&CK supplied a shared vocabulary for adversary behaviour, so summaries described detections in terms analysts already used4.

The hard part: an assistant that reads attacker-controlled text

Most AI copilots read trusted documents. A security copilot reads email subjects, file names, command lines and web requests, many written by attackers. Prompt injection, listed in the OWASP Top 10 for LLM applications5, is not a theoretical risk here. The design assumed it would be attempted:

  • All event content treated as untrusted data, clearly separated from instructions in every prompt.
  • Tools read-only by default, with narrow scopes; no tool able to change a system directly.
  • Action proposals limited to steps from approved runbooks, and every proposal approved by an analyst.
  • Generated queries shown to the analyst, so the reasoning can be checked rather than trusted.
  • An evaluation set of past incidents, including deliberately manipulated log content, run before each change.

In a SOC, the AI's input is partly written by the adversary. Design as if every log line is trying to give your copilot orders.

The general controls are covered in prompt injection defence for agents and evaluating AI agents.

How it ran

Key decisions and trade-offs

DecisionAlternativeWhy
Normalise to OCSF firstLet the model read raw vendor formatsConsistent answers and reusable queries across sources
Read-only tools by defaultGive the copilot SOAR accessLimits the damage from errors or manipulation
Approval for every actionAuto-contain high-confidence alertsKeeps accountability with analysts while trust is built
Show generated queriesShow only the answerAnalysts can verify reasoning and learn the data
Map to the IR frameworkCopilot-specific workflowFits existing audits and reporting

Incident records and handoffs were aligned with NIST SP 800-61 Revision 3, which organises incident response recommendations around the Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 functions1, so the copilot fitted the process auditors already expected. Lessons from incidents fed the approach in AI incident postmortems.

What I'd do again, and differently

Again: normalise data and build the evaluation set from real incidents before writing prompts. Differently: start runbook clean-up earlier. Many proposals were only as good as the runbooks behind them, and some runbooks were out of date.

item.title: One knowledge base, two languages: a bilingual Arabic and English assistant for UAE customers
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: How a UAE service organisation can answer customers in Arabic and English from one knowledge base: bilingual retrieval, dialect handling, citations and data residency.
item.content:encoded:
A UAE utility's customers asked the same questions in Gulf Arabic, Modern Standard Arabic, English and a mix of all three. Its knowledge lived in policies written in one language or the other. The goal was an assistant that answers in the customer's language, from the right source, with a citation, and keeps personal data in the country.

The situation

A UAE utility handled a large volume of customer questions about bills, connections, moving home and service interruptions. Customers wrote in Modern Standard Arabic, Gulf Arabic, English, and frequently a mix of Arabic and English in the same message, sometimes in Latin script. The knowledge base was inconsistent: some policies existed only in English, some only in Arabic, and translations drifted out of date.

An earlier chatbot pilot had worked well in English and poorly in Arabic. Leadership wanted an assistant that treated Arabic speakers as first-class users, answered from current policy and never exposed customer data outside the country.

What had to be true

  • Answer in the customer's language, whichever language the source document was written in.
  • Cite the policy behind every answer, so agents and customers can check it.
  • Handle real Arabic: dialect, spelling variation, diacritics and code-switching.
  • Measure quality per language, not as one blended score that hides Arabic failures.
  • Keep personal data in the country and out of prompts where it isn't needed.

Architecture

The data flow, end to end

Retrieval-augmented generation grounds answers in retrieved documents rather than the model's memory, which is what makes citations possible3. Multilingual embedding models make the cross-language part work: models such as multilingual E5 were trained on large collections of multilingual text pairs so that equivalent meaning in different languages lands close together2. Embedding choice is covered in choosing embedding models and hybrid search in hybrid search for RAG.

The hard part: Arabic that real customers write

Benchmarks use clean Modern Standard Arabic. Customers don't. The work that made the difference was unglamorous:

  • Normalising letter variants and removing diacritics for keyword search, while keeping the original text for display.
  • Adding a keyword index alongside vector search, because product names, area names and account terms are often written inconsistently.
  • Building the evaluation set from real anonymised questions in Gulf Arabic, Modern Standard Arabic, English and mixed messages, scored separately.
  • Choosing the answering model on that evaluation set. Arabic-centric models such as Jais were developed precisely because Arabic is underserved, with training that combined a large Arabic corpus with English data1; the right choice is whichever performs best on your own questions.

A bilingual assistant is only as good as its worst language. Report Arabic and English quality separately, or the average will hide the problem.

The general approach to evaluation is in evaluation sets that predict production.

How it ran

Key decisions and trade-offs

DecisionAlternativeWhy
One bilingual indexSeparate Arabic and English systemsNo content gaps when a policy exists in only one language
Hybrid search with normalisationVector search onlyCatches inconsistent spellings of names and terms
Model chosen on own eval setPick the most popular modelArabic quality varies widely between models
Agent assist before customer launchLaunch to customers directlyStaff corrections improved Arabic answers safely
Redact before the model, host in countrySend full messages to a foreign APISimplifies data protection and transfer obligations

The federal Personal Data Protection Law governs personal data processing in the UAE4. Commentary notes it does not apply in the DIFC and ADGM free zones or to health data covered by separate law, and that transfers abroad are generally limited to jurisdictions with adequate protection5. Redaction and in-country hosting kept the design simple under those rules; see UAE PDPL and AI architecture.

What I'd do again, and differently

Again: build the bilingual evaluation set first and launch to agents before customers. Differently: involve content owners earlier. Many "Arabic quality" problems were really missing or outdated Arabic source content, not model weaknesses.

item.title: Building a fintech platform for UAE Open Finance: consent, security and a single hub
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: How a UAE fintech can connect to the Central Bank's Open Finance API hub: consent flows, FAPI-grade security, data minimisation and an architecture ready for new use cases.
item.content:encoded:
A UAE fintech had built its product on screen scraping and one-off bank integrations. The Central Bank's Open Finance framework offered a regulated, standardised alternative through a central API hub. The goal was to re-platform around consent and secure APIs without stalling the product roadmap.

The situation

A fintech serving customers in the UAE offered budgeting and cash-flow insights built on account data. Getting that data had meant a patchwork: screen scraping for some banks, bilateral integrations with others, and manual statement uploads as a fallback. Each connection broke differently, security reviews were difficult to pass, and the approach had no future as regulation matured.

The Central Bank of the UAE's Open Finance Regulation changed the picture by establishing a regulated framework for open finance services1. The question for leadership was how to move onto it cleanly, while continuing to ship features.

What had to be true

  • One integration path through the regulated framework, replacing scraping and bespoke connectors.
  • Consent as a product feature: customers see what they shared, with whom, for how long, and can revoke it.
  • Financial-grade security that a bank's or regulator's reviewer would recognise.
  • Data minimisation: store only what each feature needs, for as long as it needs it.
  • Clear regulatory boundaries, including where free zone permissions do and do not apply.

The framework is described as having three parts: a trust framework, an API hub and common infrastructure services2. Commentary highlights that the API hub is operated by a Central Bank subsidiary, Nebras, as a single gateway between providers and licensed institutions, that participation is mandatory for licensees in respect of in-scope products, and that DFSA or FSRA permissions in the financial free zones do not by themselves grant access to the onshore hub3.

Architecture

The data flow, end to end

The hard part: security that reviewers recognise

Financial APIs attract determined attackers, and generic OAuth setups leave room for token theft and replay. The OpenID Foundation's FAPI 2.0 security profile defines a hardened profile of OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect for exactly these APIs; its security profile and attacker model were approved as final specifications, and conformance tests and certification are available45. Building to a recognised profile meant security discussions with partners started from a shared baseline rather than a custom design.

  • Sender-constrained tokens and strong client authentication, so a stolen token alone is not enough.
  • Keys held in a key management service or hardware security module, never in application configuration.
  • Conformance testing in CI against the profile, run before every release of the connector.
  • Product services given no direct access to tokens or the hub; they consume events and minimised data.

In open finance, consent is not a checkbox. It is the primary key of the whole data model: every token, fetch and stored field should trace back to one.

How it ran

Key decisions and trade-offs

DecisionAlternativeWhy
Integrate through the regulated hubKeep bilateral and scraped connectionsOne standard path, a regulated basis and fewer breakages
Consent service as a core domainConsent flags on user recordsPurpose, scope, expiry and revocation need their own model
Build to FAPI 2.0Generic OAuth setupRecognised baseline for financial APIs, with conformance tests
Minimise at ingestionStore everything, filter laterLess risk, simpler retention and easier privacy answers
Tokens isolated from product servicesServices call the hub directlySmaller attack surface and one place to audit

What I'd do again, and differently

Again: treat consent as the centre of the data model and build to a recognised security profile from the start. Differently: settle the licensing and regulatory perimeter before detailed design, especially the onshore and free zone question. It shaped which institutions and products were reachable more than any technical choice. Related reading: UAE PDPL and AI architecture and idempotent payment pipelines.

item.title: Taming a multi-cloud Terraform estate: modules, state, secrets and a paved road
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: How a company running AWS, Azure and GCP can turn sprawling Terraform into composed modules, small state, safe secrets, policy checks and a paved road for teams.
item.content:encoded:
Years of acquisitions and team autonomy had left infrastructure across three clouds, described by hundreds of Terraform folders with copied modules, giant state files and secrets in plaintext. Changes were slow and frightening. The goal was an estate that teams could change quickly and safely, without a central bottleneck.

The situation

A company had grown partly through acquisitions, and each acquired team had brought its own cloud and its own way of using Terraform. The result was infrastructure across AWS, Azure and GCP, described by hundreds of folders. Modules had been copied rather than shared, so fixes landed in one place and not the others. Some state files described entire environments, so a careless plan could touch hundreds of resources. Database passwords and keys sat in state, readable by anyone with access to the bucket.

Engineers had learned to avoid infrastructure changes. That was the real cost: features waited on a handful of people brave enough to run apply.

What had to be true

  • Small, composable modules per cloud, versioned and shared, rather than copies.
  • Small blast radius: no single plan able to damage unrelated systems.
  • No plaintext secrets in state, and narrow access to state that remains.
  • Every change through a pipeline, with plan review and policy checks; no laptop applies to production.
  • Teams self-serve common infrastructure through a paved road, with the platform team owning the road, not every change.

Architecture

The data flow, end to end

The hard part: resisting the universal module

The first instinct was a set of cloud-agnostic modules: one "database" module that worked on all three clouds. It would have hidden the features that made each managed service worth using and created a large abstraction nobody could debug. HashiCorp's guidance favours composition instead: a root module assembling small building blocks and passing dependencies between them as inputs and outputs1.

  • Building blocks were provider-specific, thin and opinionated about security defaults.
  • Shared interfaces covered what really is common: naming, tagging, ownership labels and output shapes.
  • Templates composed blocks into patterns teams actually use, such as "service with database and queue".
  • Each block had examples and tests, and was released with semantic versions.

Secrets were the other urgent fix. Terraform 1.10 introduced ephemeral values that are not persisted in plan or state, and 1.11 added write-only arguments on managed resources, so secrets can flow from a secrets manager into resources without landing in state23. Every secret that had ever been in state was rotated as part of the move. The checklist is in keeping secrets out of Terraform state.

Multi-cloud doesn't need multi-cloud modules. It needs consistent interfaces, good building blocks for each cloud, and one way to ship changes.

How it ran

Key decisions and trade-offs

DecisionAlternativeWhy
Provider-specific building blocksUniversal cross-cloud modulesKeeps each service's strengths and stays debuggable
State split by blast radius and ownerOne state per environmentLimits damage and lets access follow ownership
Pipeline-only appliesEngineers apply from laptopsConsistent, reviewed and auditable changes
Ephemeral values and write-only secretsMark secrets as sensitiveSensitive hides values from output; it doesn't keep them out of state
Modules compatible with Terraform and OpenTofuCommit to one tool nowKeeps the licensing decision open without blocking work

The tooling question came up early. OpenTofu was forked from Terraform under the Linux Foundation after HashiCorp's 2023 licence change4. Rather than let that decision block the refactor, modules were kept compatible with both while legal and procurement reached a view; the trade-offs are in OpenTofu or Terraform in 2026.

What I'd do again, and differently

Again: put pipelines, policy and state boundaries in place before migrating anything, and rotate every secret that touched state. Differently: publish the module interface conventions (names, tags and outputs) in the first week. Teams started writing new stacks immediately, and every one written before the conventions existed needed rework. More on structure in Terraform module design for multi-cloud.

item.title: One AI governance programme that answers buyers in the EU, US and UAE
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: How an AI software company can answer EU AI Act, SOC 2 and enterprise AI questionnaires from one programme: inventory, ISO 42001, NIST AI RMF and evidence by design.
item.content:encoded:
An AI software company was losing weeks in every enterprise deal to security and AI questionnaires, each asking for the same things in different words. Regulation was moving in three markets at once. The goal was one governance programme whose evidence could be reused for every buyer, auditor and regulator.

The situation

An AI software company sold to enterprises in Europe, the United States and the Gulf. Its products used large language models for summarisation, classification and agent-style automation. Every serious deal now came with a security questionnaire, an AI questionnaire and often a data protection review. The questions overlapped heavily but never matched exactly, so the CTO and a few senior engineers answered them by hand, deal after deal.

Meanwhile the rules kept moving. The EU AI Act's obligations were phasing in, then partly delayed; US buyers asked about SOC 2 and the NIST AI framework; Gulf buyers asked about data residency and local regulation. The company needed one answer, not three.

What had to be true

  • One inventory of every AI system and feature, with owner, purpose, models, data and risk rating.
  • One control set, mapped to each framework, rather than a programme per regulation.
  • Evidence by design: logs, evaluations and approvals produced by the delivery pipeline, not gathered by hand.
  • Proportionate: governance effort matched to risk, so low-risk features ship without ceremony.
  • Owned by engineering and product, with legal and security as partners rather than gatekeepers.

Architecture

The data flow, end to end

The frameworks fit together better than their language suggests. The NIST AI Risk Management Framework organises AI risk work into govern, map, measure and manage functions4. ISO/IEC 42001 specifies a certifiable AI management system3. SOC 2 reports on controls against the trust services criteria for service organisations5. One control can satisfy all three when it is written once and mapped carefully, as discussed in ISO 42001 vs the NIST AI RMF and SOC 2 for AI startups.

The hard part: a moving regulatory timeline

The EU AI Act applies different obligations at different times1. AI literacy duties already applied6, transparency obligations under Article 50 applied from 2 August 2026, and, as reported after the Digital Omnibus, stand-alone high-risk obligations moved to December 2027 with Annex I products following in August 20282. Building for a single deadline would have meant rework every time it moved.

  • Obligations were attached to inventory entries by role and use case, not to a calendar, so a date change updated a field, not a plan.
  • Controls that are valuable regardless of deadlines, such as inventory, evaluation, logging and human oversight, were built first.
  • High-risk-specific controls were designed early but switched on per product as classification and timelines firmed up.
  • Each EU AI Act question was tracked as provider or deployer, because the obligations differ.

Build governance around capabilities, not deadlines. Inventories, evaluations and logs are useful under every regime; dates change, capabilities stay.

The background is in the Digital Omnibus roadmap, when fine-tuning makes you a provider and, for Gulf buyers, the UAE's Federal Authority for AI and Data.

How it ran

Key decisions and trade-offs

DecisionAlternativeWhy
One control set, many mappingsA programme per frameworkLess duplication; new rules become mapping updates
Evidence from pipelinesEvidence gathered for each auditAlways current, cheaper, and more credible
Proportionate risk tiersSame process for every featureKeeps low-risk delivery fast and attention on what matters
Capabilities before deadlinesPlan around one regulatory dateSurvives timeline changes without rework
Public trust centreAnswer every questionnaire from scratchBuyers self-serve the common answers

What I'd do again, and differently

Again: start with the inventory and let engineering pipelines produce the evidence. Differently: involve sales engineering from the start. They see every questionnaire, and their list of repeated questions is the fastest way to prioritise which controls and evidence to build first.

item.title: One governed clinical trial data platform, from site data to submission datasets
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: How a biotech can unify trial data from EDC, labs and devices into one governed platform, with lineage to SDTM submissions and audit trails for GCP and Part 11.
item.content:encoded:
A growing biotech ran several trials through different vendors: an EDC system, central labs, eCOA, wearables and imaging. Each study rebuilt its data pipelines from scratch, and the path from raw data to submission datasets lived in programmers' heads. The goal was one platform with lineage, quality and audit trails built in.

The situation

A biotech with several programmes in clinical development worked, like most of its peers, through vendors: one for electronic data capture, others for central labs, patient-reported outcomes, wearable devices and imaging. Each study's data team built its own transfers, mappings and checks. Submission datasets were produced by statistical programmers working from extracts, and the reasoning behind many transformations existed only in their code and memory.

As the pipeline grew, leadership saw the risk: every new study cost the same effort as the last, and an inspection question about where a value came from could take days to answer.

What had to be true

  • Traceability from every submission value back to its source record and every transformation in between.
  • Reuse across studies: shared ingestion, mapping patterns and checks, not bespoke pipelines per protocol.
  • Quality visible early, to data managers during the study, not at database lock.
  • Audit trails and access control by design, suitable for computerised system validation.
  • Vendor independence: changing an EDC or lab vendor should not mean rebuilding the platform.

The regulatory direction supported this. ICH finalised the revised Good Clinical Practice guideline, E6(R3), in January 2025, and commentary highlights its risk-proportionate approach and a new data governance section that acknowledges digital trial data handling1. In the EU, the principles and Annex 1 applied from 23 July 20252.

Architecture

The data flow, end to end

Submission requirements anchored the design. The FDA lists the study data standards it supports and requires, including SDTM versions, with dates from which each version is supported and then required3. Building SDTM mappings as versioned, reviewable assets meant a standards update became a controlled change rather than a scramble.

The hard part: one mapping layer for many protocols

Every protocol is different, and the temptation is to treat every study as a special case. The platform separated what genuinely varies by study, such as visit schedules, endpoints and specific forms, from what doesn't, such as demographics, adverse events, concomitant medications and lab structures.

  • A shared library of mappings and derivations for common domains, with study-level extensions rather than copies.
  • Controlled terminology managed centrally, so the same concept is coded the same way across studies.
  • Mapping specifications stored with the code, reviewed like code and versioned with each data cut.
  • Blinded and unblinded data separated by access control and environment, not convention.

The question an inspector asks is simple: where did this number come from? A platform is ready when anyone on the team can answer it in minutes.

How it ran

Key decisions and trade-offs

DecisionAlternativeWhy
Immutable raw zone per transferOverwrite with latest vendor fileAny result can be reproduced from the exact data received
Mappings as versioned codeSpecifications in spreadsheetsReviewable, testable and traceable changes
Shared library with study extensionsCopy and modify per studyFixes and standards updates apply everywhere
Checks during the studyClean-up before lockIssues resolved with sites while they are fresh
Audit trail designed inRely on system logsPart 11 expects secure, time-stamped audit trails of record changes

For systems that create or modify records required by FDA regulations, 21 CFR Part 11 sets expectations for electronic records, including secure, computer-generated, time-stamped audit trails4. Designing those in from the first phase was far cheaper than retrofitting them.

What I'd do again, and differently

Again: one study end to end before building the shared library, and quality at the table from the first week. Differently: negotiate transfer agreements with vendors as part of platform work, not study start-up. Consistent vendor formats are what make shared mappings possible. Related approaches are in data contracts and FHIR to OMOP architecture.

item.title: From spreadsheets to an auditable pharmacovigilance signal platform
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: How a pharma safety team can combine spontaneous reports, literature and real-world data on OMOP to detect, prioritise and evaluate safety signals with an audit trail.
item.content:encoded:
A drug safety team tracked potential signals across spreadsheets, email and slide decks. Each evaluation meant a bespoke data request and weeks of analysis. The goal was one platform that detects candidate signals, keeps the reasoning auditable and lets the team test them quickly against real-world data.

The situation

A pharmaceutical company's drug safety team handled case processing well; their safety database and regulatory reporting were mature. Signal management was not. Potential signals arrived from periodic report reviews, literature, partners and occasional regulator queries, and were tracked in a spreadsheet. Evaluating one meant a custom data request, an analyst working for weeks, and conclusions summarised in slides that did not record which data or method they came from.

The head of safety wanted three things: consistent screening, faster evaluation and a record any inspector could follow from first observation to final decision.

What had to be true

  • Every signal has one record, from source to decision, with who did what and why.
  • Screening is consistent: the same methods on the same schedule, not ad hoc queries.
  • Detection is not confused with evidence. Report counts start investigations; they don't conclude them.
  • Evaluation is fast and reproducible, using standardised real-world data and versioned study code.
  • Validated where it matters, with the computerised system controls a regulated safety function expects.

The EU's good pharmacovigilance practice guidance on signal management frames the lifecycle the platform needed to support, and EMA presentations on it emphasise that marketing authorisation holders should keep an audit trail of their signal management activities1.

Architecture

The data flow, end to end

The hard part: not over-reading spontaneous reports

Spontaneous reports are the backbone of signal detection and also easy to misuse. The FDA states plainly that a report does not mean the product caused the event, that report counts cannot establish how often an event occurs, and that reports can be duplicated, incomplete or stimulated by publicity2. The platform's design reflected that:

  • Disproportionality scores were labelled as screening statistics, never as risk estimates, everywhere they appeared.
  • Every flag required case-level review by a safety physician before becoming a validated signal.
  • Evaluation used designed studies on population data, not more report counting.

For evaluation, self-controlled designs suited many acute safety questions because they compare time periods within the same people, removing confounding by stable characteristics3. Negative control outcomes and empirical calibration showed whether residual bias could explain a result4. The designs are compared in real-world evidence study designs.

A signal platform's most important feature is the line it draws between "worth investigating" and "evidence of harm". Blur that line and you get both false alarms and false reassurance.

How it ran

Key decisions and trade-offs

DecisionAlternativeWhy
Tracker before analyticsStart with detection algorithmsAudit trail and consistency were the biggest gaps
Physician validation of every flagAuto-open signals above a thresholdScreening statistics are not evidence of harm
OMOP for evaluation dataBespoke extracts per questionReusable study packages across data partners
Negative controls by defaultReport estimates aloneShows when bias could explain a result
Separate detection and evaluation layersOne combined risk scoreKeeps the reasoning legible to inspectors

What I'd do again, and differently

Again: fix the record-keeping first, then add analytics. Differently: agree data access with real-world data partners at the start. Contracts and governance for external data take longer than building the screening pipeline, and evaluations wait on them. The data side is described in federated health analytics and OMOP data quality checks.

item.title: Shipping AI features with evidence: a shared evaluation and observability platform
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: How a software company with many AI features can ship model and prompt changes safely: shared eval sets, release gates, OpenTelemetry GenAI tracing and cost per feature.
item.content:encoded:
Several product teams had shipped AI features, each with its own prompts, its own vendor calls and its own idea of 'good'. Model upgrades were risky, regressions were found by customers, and nobody could say what an AI feature cost to run. The goal was one platform for evaluating, releasing and observing every LLM feature.

The situation

A software company had moved quickly on AI. Support had an answer assistant, sales had an email drafter, the core product had a summariser and a natural-language search box. Each team had picked prompts, vendors and settings independently. When a model provider released a new version, nobody knew which features would get better and which would quietly break. Quality problems surfaced as customer tickets. Finance saw one large model invoice and could not split it by feature.

Leadership did not want to slow the teams down. They wanted the same confidence in AI releases that they already had in ordinary code releases.

What had to be true

  • Every AI feature has an evaluation set that reflects real use, owned by the team that ships it.
  • Changes ship through gates: a prompt, model or retrieval change runs the evals before it reaches customers.
  • Every model and tool call is traceable, with latency, tokens and errors, using an open standard rather than a vendor format.
  • Sensitive content is not logged by default.
  • Cost and quality are visible per feature, so product managers can make trade-offs.

Architecture

The data flow, end to end

Tracing followed the OpenTelemetry semantic conventions for generative AI, which standardise how model calls are recorded, including the model, input and output token counts and, when explicitly enabled, prompt and completion content12. Standard metrics for token usage and operation duration made cost and latency comparable across features and vendors3. The detail is in LLM observability with OpenTelemetry.

The hard part: evaluation sets that predict production

Building the pipeline was straightforward. Building evaluation sets that actually predicted how features behaved for customers was not. Generic benchmarks said little about whether the support assistant would answer a specific customer's question correctly.

  • Cases drawn from real, anonymised usage, grouped by intent, with a slice of known hard and sensitive cases.
  • Deterministic checks wherever possible: format, required fields, citations present, forbidden content absent.
  • Rubric-based model graders only where judgement was needed, calibrated against human labels. Research on LLM-as-a-judge found strong models can match human preference agreement, but also documented position and verbosity biases that need controlling4.
  • Regular refresh from production misses, so the set evolves with the product.

More on this in evaluation sets that predict production and, for agentic features, evaluating AI agents.

An eval set is a product artefact, not a test fixture. The team that owns the feature owns its definition of good.

How it ran

Key decisions and trade-offs

DecisionAlternativeWhy
OpenTelemetry GenAI conventionsA vendor-specific tracing SDKPortable across vendors and backends, fits existing observability
Content capture off by defaultLog everything for debuggingPrompts and tool arguments can hold sensitive data
Deterministic checks before judgesJudge every output with a modelCheaper, faster and free of judge bias
Eval sets owned by feature teamsCentral QA writes all evalsTeams know what good looks like for their users
Gateway for all model callsEach team calls vendors directlyOne place for keys, routing, limits and cost attribution

The programme was mapped to the NIST Generative AI Profile, which gave the risk team a recognised structure for issues such as confabulation, information security and data privacy5.

What I'd do again, and differently

Again: start with tracing and cost per feature, because visibility creates demand for evaluation. Differently: write a model upgrade playbook in the first phase. Provider version changes arrive on their schedule, not yours, and a rehearsed path from new model to gated rollout takes the drama out of them.

item.title: Making Kubernetes spend visible, owned and controllable, without slowing teams down
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: How a scale-up can make Kubernetes spend visible and controllable per team: cost allocation, right-sizing without restarts, scale to zero, quotas and a paved road.
item.content:encoded:
Cloud bills were growing faster than the business, and nobody could say which team or product drove the increase. The goal was a platform where every workload has an owner, a cost, sensible defaults and a cheap way to shrink, so cost becomes a product decision rather than a quarterly panic.

The situation

A fast-growing technology company ran most of its products on a handful of shared Kubernetes clusters. Teams shipped quickly, which was the point. But cloud spend had become one of the largest lines in the budget, and the monthly review was a guessing game: the bill showed compute, storage and network by account, while the organisation thought in teams and products. Requests and limits had been copied between services for years. Some workloads ran around the clock for jobs that happened once a day.

A previous clean-up project had cut costs for a quarter, then spend crept back. The leadership question was simple: how do we make this stay fixed?

What had to be true

  • Every workload has an owner: a team and a product, enforced, not hoped for.
  • Cost is visible where decisions are made: per team, per product, in a format finance accepts.
  • Efficiency is the default: new services start right-sized and autoscaled without teams becoming Kubernetes experts.
  • Shrinking is cheap and safe, so teams actually do it.
  • No slowdown in delivery; controls live in the paved road, not in tickets.

Architecture

The data flow, end to end

OpenCost provides workload-level cost allocation for Kubernetes, attributing cluster costs to namespaces, labels and workloads1. Joining those allocations with billing data in the FinOps Foundation's FOCUS format gave finance and engineering one view of the same numbers2; the reasoning is in FOCUS and AI spend.

The hard part: making shrinking safe

Visibility alone rarely changes behaviour. Teams knew some services were over-provisioned; they left them because changing requests meant restarts, and restarts meant risk. Two Kubernetes changes removed most of that friction:

  • In-place Pod resize, stable since Kubernetes 1.35, lets CPU and memory change on running Pods, and the Vertical Pod Autoscaler's in-place mode uses it3. Recommendations could finally be applied continuously, starting with CPU on stateless services. Details in in-place Pod resize.
  • Scale to zero with the HorizontalPodAutoscaler, available from Kubernetes 1.37 for workloads driven by suitable object or external metrics such as queue length4. Workers that waited idle most of the day stopped costing anything while idle. See Kubernetes FinOps and scale to zero.

Namespace quotas then capped the total each team could request, which turned capacity into a visible, negotiable budget rather than an unlimited pool5.

Cost programmes fail when saving money is risky and spending it is free. Flip both: make shrinking safe and automatic, and make every request visible to its owner.

How it ran

Key decisions and trade-offs

DecisionAlternativeWhy
Enforce ownership labels at admissionTag clean-up campaignsUnowned workloads can't appear in the first place
Open-source allocation plus FOCUSA separate cost tool per cloudOne allocation model and one billing schema across providers
Right-size in place, CPU firstRolling restarts for every changeLower risk, so recommendations actually get applied
Scale to zero only for queue-backed workScale everything to zeroUser-facing services need warm capacity
Quotas as team budgetsUnlimited shared poolMakes capacity a visible, negotiated decision

What I'd do again, and differently

Again: start with ownership and allocation, and put every improvement into the templates so it spreads automatically. Differently: agree unit cost metrics with product leaders earlier. Cost per team tells you who spends; cost per customer action tells you whether the spend is worth it.

item.title: From MCP servers on laptops to a governed enterprise agent platform
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: How an enterprise can move from ad hoc MCP servers on laptops to a governed agent platform: a private registry, central identity, scoped tokens, gateways and audit.
item.content:encoded:
Engineers had connected assistants to dozens of MCP servers, some internal, some from the internet, most with broad tokens. Security wanted to stop it; product teams wanted more of it. The goal was a platform that made the approved path the easiest one.

The situation

An organisation had embraced AI assistants faster than it had governed them. Developers connected IDE assistants to MCP servers for the code host, the ticketing system and the data warehouse. Some servers were built internally in an afternoon; others were installed from public repositories. Many used personal access tokens with wide permissions, stored in local configuration files. Nobody could say which servers were in use, who had approved them, or what they had done.

Security's first instinct was to block MCP outright. Leadership's instinct was the opposite: agents were becoming central to engineering and operations, and a ban would simply push usage further out of sight.

What had to be true

  • One place to find approved servers, discoverable by the clients people already use.
  • No long-lived shared tokens. Access flows through the identity provider, per user, with the narrowest scopes that work.
  • Every tool call is attributable to a person, an agent, a server and a version.
  • Writes and destructive actions need explicit, visible consent.
  • Publishing a new internal server is easy if it follows the standard; exceptions are rare and visible.

Architecture

The design followed the ecosystem's own shape: the official MCP Registry is intended as an upstream that organisations build private subregistries on, adding internal servers that should never appear publicly3. The approach is described in more depth in running an enterprise MCP registry.

The data flow, end to end

Step five matters most. The MCP security guidance names token passthrough, where a server forwards a token it received from the client to a downstream API, as an anti-pattern that breaks OAuth security boundaries, and the authorisation specification forbids it12. Every server on the platform validates that tokens were issued for it, and calls downstream systems with its own, separately scoped credentials.

The hard part: scopes people would actually accept

The technical controls were well understood. The difficult part was scope design. The MCP guidance warns that over-broad scopes granted up front expand the blast radius of a stolen token, make revocation disruptive and create consent dialogs that users abandon; it recommends a progressive, least-privilege model starting with a minimal read-only set1. In practice that meant:

  • A small, named set of scopes per server, starting with read-only discovery.
  • Write and admin scopes requested only when a user first invokes a tool that needs them.
  • Central control through the identity provider using the authorisation extensions, so administrators can grant and revoke access in one place4.
  • Metrics on which scopes are requested and used, so creep is visible.

Least privilege only works if the least-privilege path is also the least-friction path. Otherwise people find a personal token and work around it.

How it ran

Key decisions and trade-offs

DecisionAlternativeWhy
Private registry mirroring the public oneAllow-list in a wikiClients can discover from it, and versions can be pinned
Gateway in front of remote serversEach server enforces policy aloneOne place for authentication, policy, rate limits and audit
Servers use their own downstream credentialsPass client tokens throughToken passthrough is forbidden and breaks audit and audience checks
Progressive scopesGrant everything at first loginSmaller blast radius and consent people actually read
Enforce after migrationBlock first, build laterAvoids pushing usage underground

The prompt injection and excessive agency risks in the OWASP Top 10 for LLM applications shaped the server template, with tool descriptions treated as untrusted and write tools gated by consent5. The detailed controls are in securing MCP servers, prompt injection defence for agents and MCP extensions strategy.

What I'd do again, and differently

Again: start with an inventory and make the approved path faster than the unapproved one before enforcing anything. Differently: publish the server template and its CI checks in the first phase. Teams wanted to build compliant servers early, and every week without a template produced another one-off that later needed migrating.

item.title: AI-assisted claims triage that adjusters trust and regulators can audit
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: How a US insurer can triage first notice of loss with AI while keeping adjusters in control: document extraction, routing, fraud signals and an auditable AI programme.
item.content:encoded:
Claims arrive as phone notes, emails, photos and PDFs. Triage decides which adjuster sees what, how fast, and with which flags. The goal was to use AI to do that first pass well, without letting a model decide anyone's claim, and with a governance programme ready for state regulators.

The situation

A multi-line insurer in the United States handled first notice of loss through a mix of call centre notes, web forms, emails with attachments and broker submissions. Triage was manual: a team read each new claim, decided its complexity, picked a queue and flagged anything suspicious. At peaks, the backlog meant simple claims waited behind complex ones, and the quality of triage depended on who happened to read the file.

Leadership wanted AI in the loop. The claims and compliance teams wanted something else first: confidence that no model would quietly decide a claim, and evidence they could show a regulator about how AI was governed.

What had to be true

  • Adjusters decide. AI summarises, extracts and suggests; coverage, payment and denial decisions stay with licensed staff.
  • Every flag has a reason a person can read and challenge.
  • Testing for error and unfair outcomes before release and on a schedule, by line of business.
  • One inventory of AI systems with owners, purpose, data and controls.
  • No change to the claims system of record; AI writes suggestions alongside it, not into it.

These map closely to the NAIC model bulletin, which asks insurers to maintain a written programme for the responsible use of AI systems, including governance, risk management controls and testing for errors, bias and unfair discrimination1. A growing number of states have adopted it, so building to it was the safest baseline across jurisdictions23.

Architecture

The data flow, end to end

Extraction used structured outputs validated against a schema, so a malformed response fails fast rather than reaching an adjuster, the pattern described in structured outputs for reliable LLM integration. Fraud signals drew on relationships between parties, addresses, repairers and prior claims, using the graph approach in entity resolution for knowledge graphs.

The hard part: fairness and explainability, not extraction

Getting a model to read a claim form well is now the easy part. The difficult questions were about outcomes. Does a fraud signal fire more often for claims from certain postcodes for reasons unrelated to fraud? Does a severity hint systematically under-prioritise one line of business? The bulletin expects insurers to test for exactly these risks1, and the NIST AI Risk Management Framework gave a practical structure for mapping, measuring and managing them4.

  • An evaluation set of historical claims with known outcomes, refreshed regularly, scored for extraction accuracy and routing agreement.
  • Outcome comparisons across segments the compliance team defined, reviewed before each release.
  • Fraud signals limited to features the special investigations team could explain, with every flag showing its contributing reasons.
  • Override rates tracked by signal; a signal adjusters routinely override gets investigated, not ignored.

Adjuster overrides are the most valuable data in a claims AI programme. They show, in real time, where the model and the experts disagree.

How it ran

Key decisions and trade-offs

DecisionAlternativeWhy
AI suggests, adjusters decideStraight-through automationKeeps accountability with licensed staff and simplifies regulatory answers
Rules for complexity, models for readingOne end-to-end modelRouting logic stays readable and changeable by claims ops
Shadow mode firstLaunch with suggestions liveMeasured agreement before influencing anyone
Explainable fraud featuresOpaque anomaly scoresInvestigators can act on, and challenge, a reason
Build to the NAIC bulletin everywhereState-by-state variantsOne programme, mapped to each state's adoption

For insurers with European operations, the EU AI Act adds another layer: its Annex III lists AI used for risk assessment and pricing of natural persons in life and health insurance as high-risk5. Claims triage sits next to that boundary, so classification should be confirmed with counsel; the governance described here is a strong starting point either way. See ISO 42001 vs the NIST AI RMF and Colorado's AI law reset for the wider landscape.

What I'd do again, and differently

Again: write the AI programme and the evaluation set before writing the first prompt, and run in shadow mode. Differently: involve the special investigations team in designing fraud signals from the first week. Their sense of what makes a signal actionable shaped the design more than any model choice.
